title: Growth Marketing: Funnels, Experiments and Sustainable Growth
subtitle: Find where a business loses customers, test fixes with fair experiments, and turn honest results into growth and paid consulting work.
description: An advanced, practical course for marketers and business owners who already know digital marketing basics. You will map AARRR funnels, calculate unit economics, design and prioritise experiments, check results for statistical significance, and package audits, proposals and case studies for clients in Nigeria and beyond.
outcomes: Map a business on the AARRR funnel with real numbers and identify the biggest leak
Choose a North Star metric and judge channels with CAC, LTV and payback
Build a cohort table and an experiment log from free tools
Design, prioritise (ICE/RICE) and size experiments, then check results with a z-test and guardrails
Run a growth audit, price and scope a proposal, and protect client data
Publish honest case studies and a 90-day growth roadmap
audience: Women with basic digital marketing experience who want to grow their own business or offer growth marketing to start-ups and small brands.
tools: Google Sheets (free) and a Google account
Access to a business's Instagram Insights, Meta Ads Manager, Google Analytics 4, WhatsApp Business and payment exports (with permission)
A calculator and an online A/B test significance or sample-size calculator

modules.title: Growth Foundations: Funnels, Metrics and Levers
modules.overview: Growth marketing treats the whole customer journey as one system you can measure and improve. In this module you map a real funnel with the AARRR model, find the stage that leaks most, choose a North Star metric backed by unit economics, and learn the growth levers that work in WhatsApp-first, trust-sensitive African markets.

lessons.title: From campaigns to growth systems: the AARRR funnel and finding the leak
objectives: Explain how growth marketing differs from running one-off campaigns
Map a business onto the five AARRR stages with a real number at each stage
Calculate stage-to-stage conversion rates and spot the biggest leak
Estimate which improvement is worth more before spending any money

blocks.text: A campaign asks: how many people did my advert reach? Growth marketing asks a wider question: **of everyone who heard about us, how many became happy, paying, returning customers, and how many brought friends?** It looks at the whole journey as one system, finds the weakest point, and fixes it with small, measured experiments. A business can double its sales without spending more on adverts if it stops losing people after they arrive.

This course assumes you already know marketing basics such as reach, click-through rate and UTM links. Here we go a level deeper: funnel analysis, unit economics, experiment design, honest statistics and selling growth work as a professional.
The AARRR funnel

In 2007 the investor Dave McClure described five stages every customer passes through, nicknamed the "pirate metrics" because the initials spell AARRR. Some teams put Revenue before Referral; the order matters less than measuring all five.

head: Stage
Question it answers
Typical measure
rows: Profile visits, website sessions, WhatsApp chats started
Do they have a good first experience?
First order, first lesson completed, account funded
Customers who referred at least one new buyer
Do we make money from them?
Revenue and gross profit per customer

blocks.title: The AARRR customer journey
items: Acquisition: they find you
Activation: first good experience
Retention: they return
Referral: they invite others
Revenue: you profit
blocks.caption: Each arrow is a place where people drop out, and each drop is a possible experiment.

blocks.text: Turning a funnel into numbers

A funnel is only useful when every stage has a number for the same period, usually one month. Divide each stage by the stage before it to get the **step conversion rate**. The stage with a low rate and a cheap fix is usually your best opportunity, not automatically the stage with the lowest number.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding the leak in a meal-prep business
blocks.context: For example, Ada sells weekly meal-prep packs in Lekki, Lagos, through Instagram and WhatsApp. An average order is about ₦12,000 (illustrative). She pulls last month's numbers from Instagram Insights, WhatsApp Business labels and her Paystack dashboard.
steps: Acquisition: 1,200 Instagram profile visits led to 300 WhatsApp chats. Step rate = 300 ÷ 1,200 = 25%.
Activation: 90 of the 300 chats became a first paid order. Step rate = 90 ÷ 300 = 30%.
Retention: 27 of the 90 first-time buyers ordered again within 30 days. Step rate = 27 ÷ 90 = 30%.
Referral: 9 of the 90 buyers sent a friend who ordered. Step rate = 9 ÷ 90 = 10%.
She models two fixes. Raising chat-to-order from 30% to 35% gives 300 × 0.35 = 105 first orders, 15 more per month, worth about 15 × ₦12,000 = ₦180,000.
Raising 30-day repeat from 30% to 40% gives 90 × 0.40 = 36 repeat buyers, 9 more per month, but each of those customers may keep buying for months, so the value builds up.
She reads 30 chats that did not convert. Most asked about delivery days and never got a clear reply. That points to a cheap fix: a quick reply with the menu, prices and delivery schedule.
blocks.result: Ada's first experiment targets activation (chat to first order) because she found a clear, cheap cause. Retention becomes her second experiment. She spent nothing on adverts to find this.

blocks.title: Look at people, not just percentages
blocks.text: Numbers tell you where people leave; conversations tell you why. Before you design any experiment, read at least 20 real chats, reviews or abandoned orders from the leaking stage.
Why growth teams obsess over retention

If customers do not come back, every naira spent on acquisition buys a one-time sale. When retention is strong, each new customer keeps paying, referrals rise because happy customers talk, and acquisition becomes cheaper over time. That is why experienced growth marketers check retention first: pouring adverts into a funnel that leaks after the first purchase is like filling a bucket with a hole in it.

items: **Healthy sign:** repeat buyers are a growing share of monthly orders.
**Warning sign:** sales only rise in months when you spend more on adverts.
**Fix order:** usually activation and retention first, then scale acquisition.

blocks.text: Set the window and the unit before you count

Two choices make funnel numbers comparable. First, the **time window**: use the same calendar month (or the same four weeks) for every stage, and keep it fixed when you compare later months. Second, the **unit**: count people, not actions. One customer who sends five messages is one chat, not five. If you mix people and actions, your step rates will look better or worse than they really are, and experiments built on them will aim at the wrong stage.

Write down where each number came from (Instagram Insights, WhatsApp labels, Paystack). Next month you must pull the figures from the same places in the same way, or a change in method will look like a change in performance.

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.alt: A woman studying a rising growth chart on a large screen
blocks.caption: Growth marketing starts by reading the numbers for every stage, not only the advert results.

takeaways: Growth marketing improves the whole customer journey, not just advert reach.
AARRR: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue, each with a number.
Step conversion rate = this stage ÷ previous stage.
Pick the leak with a clear cause and cheap fix; check retention before scaling ads.

activity.title: Map a real funnel
steps: Choose a business you run or can get numbers from (with the owner's permission).
Write one measure for each AARRR stage for last month.
Fill in the numbers from Instagram Insights, WhatsApp labels, sales records or Paystack/Opay/Moniepoint statements.
Calculate each step conversion rate.
Read 20 conversations from the weakest stage and note the three most common reasons people dropped out.
activity.evidence: A one-page funnel sheet with five stages, numbers, step rates and three drop-out reasons.

lessons.title: North Star metric, input metrics and unit economics
objectives: Choose a North Star metric that reflects real customer value
Break the North Star into three or four input metrics a team can act on
Calculate customer acquisition cost, lifetime value and payback period
Judge whether a channel is worth scaling using LTV to CAC

blocks.text: A growth team that watches twenty numbers improves none of them. Mature teams agree on one **North Star metric**: a single measure that rises only when customers get real value and the business grows. Under it sit a few **input metrics**, the levers the team can actually move this week.
What makes a good North Star

items: It measures value delivered to customers, not vanity (followers and likes are vanity for most sellers).
It leads revenue: when it rises, money follows within weeks.
It can be counted every week from data you already have.
Everyone on the team understands it in one sentence.

head: Business (illustrative)
Weak metric
Better North Star
rows: Customers who bought twice in 60 days
Users who made a deposit this month

blocks.title: North Star and its inputs
items: North Star: weekly repeat orders
New activated customers
Repeat purchase rate
Orders per customer
Experiments on each input
blocks.caption: The team runs experiments on the inputs at the base; the North Star at the top moves as a result.

blocks.text: Unit economics: is growth making or losing money?

Growth that loses money on every customer is not growth. Three numbers keep you honest. **Customer acquisition cost (CAC)** is what you spend to win one new customer: total marketing spend for a channel divided by new customers from that channel. **Lifetime value (LTV)** is the gross profit a customer brings over a period you choose, often 12 months: average order value × gross margin × number of orders in that period. **Payback period** is how long it takes for that customer's gross profit to repay the CAC.

blocks.title: Worked example: should Chioma scale Instagram ads?
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells shea-butter skincare from Ibadan through WhatsApp. All prices are illustrative. Last month she spent ₦150,000 on Instagram ads and won 50 new customers. Her average order is ₦10,000 and her gross margin (after product and packaging cost) is 40%. Her records show a customer buys about 3 times a year.
steps: CAC = ₦150,000 ÷ 50 = ₦3,000 per customer.
Gross profit per order = ₦10,000 × 0.40 = ₦4,000.
12-month LTV = ₦4,000 × 3 orders = ₦12,000.
LTV to CAC ratio = ₦12,000 ÷ ₦3,000 = 4 to 1.
Payback: the first order earns ₦4,000, which already covers the ₦3,000 CAC, so payback is on the first purchase.
She tests a micro-influencer channel: ₦90,000 brings 15 customers. CAC = ₦6,000. LTV to CAC = ₦12,000 ÷ ₦6,000 = 2 to 1, and payback needs 1.5 orders.
blocks.result: Instagram ads pay back immediately at 4 to 1, so Chioma can scale them carefully while watching CAC each week. The influencer channel is weaker; she keeps it small unless retention for those buyers proves higher.

blocks.title: About rules of thumb
blocks.text: Many investors use a rough guide that LTV should be about three times CAC or more. Treat it as a starting point, not a law. A business with little cash needs fast payback even more than a high ratio, because money spent on ads today must come back before stock needs restocking.
Common mistakes

items: Using revenue instead of gross profit for LTV, which can make a loss-making channel look healthy.
Dividing all spend by all customers, which hides a bad channel behind a good one. Calculate CAC per channel.
Counting returning customers as new, which makes CAC look lower than it is.
Assuming customers will buy for five years when the business is only one year old. Use the period you can actually observe.

blocks.title: CAC rises as you scale
blocks.text: The first customers from a channel are usually the cheapest. When you double the budget, CAC often climbs. Increase spend in steps (for example 20 to 30% per week) and recalculate CAC each time rather than assuming last month's figure still holds.
When payback takes several orders

Payback period is easy to calculate once you know CAC and gross profit per order: **orders needed = CAC ÷ gross profit per order**, then convert orders into time using how often customers buy. For example, if CAC is ₦8,000, gross profit per order is ₦4,000 and customers buy every two months, payback needs 2 orders, so about two to four months depending on when the first repeat order comes. During that time the business has paid for the customer but not yet earned it back, which ties up cash.

This is why a growing small business can run short of cash even when every customer is profitable in the long run. If you advise a client, show both numbers: the LTV to CAC ratio (is the customer worth it?) and the payback period (can the business afford to wait?). If payback is long, the best experiments are often in activation and retention, because they make the second order arrive sooner.

items: Recalculate LTV every quarter from real cohort data, not from hopes.
Keep a separate CAC for each channel and each month.
Share the inputs with the client so they can check your arithmetic.

blocks.name: money-bag
blocks.caption: Unit economics tells you whether each new customer adds money to the bag or takes it out.

takeaways: One North Star metric that reflects customer value; three or four input metrics beneath it.
CAC = channel spend ÷ new customers from that channel.
LTV = average order × gross margin × orders in the period.
Check LTV to CAC and payback before scaling any channel.

activity.title: Build a unit economics sheet
steps: Pick one business and propose a North Star metric; write why it reflects customer value.
List three input metrics under it.
For two acquisition channels, record last month's spend and new customers, then calculate CAC for each.
Calculate gross profit per order and a 12-month LTV from real order history.
Write a one-line verdict per channel: scale, hold or stop.
activity.evidence: A spreadsheet tab showing the North Star tree, CAC per channel, LTV, LTV to CAC and payback.

lessons.title: Growth levers that work in African markets: trust, WhatsApp and referral loops
objectives: Adapt standard growth tactics to trust, data-cost and payment realities in Nigeria
Design a WhatsApp-first activation path with fewer steps
Calculate a viral coefficient and the extra customers a referral loop produces
Spot referral fraud and scam risks before launching an incentive

blocks.text: Most growth playbooks were written for markets with cheap data, card payments and high trust in online sellers. Many Nigerian customers instead pay per megabyte, prefer bank transfer or pay-on-delivery, and have been burned by fake vendors. The principles stay the same; the levers change. Growth marketers who understand this have an edge with local startups and with international companies entering Africa.

blocks.title: Copying a foreign playbook vs adapting it
items: Imported playbook
Adapted for Nigeria
right: Real faces, reviews, business registration shown
blocks.caption: The goal at each stage is unchanged; the route is shaped by trust, data cost and payment habits.

blocks.text: Lever 1: trust removes friction at activation

items: Show proof early: customer videos, delivery photos with permission, and your Corporate Affairs Commission registration number if registered (not to be confused with CAC, customer acquisition cost).
Offer a low-risk first step: a small trial size, pay-on-delivery within your city, or a clear refund rule.
Use a verified checkout link (for example Paystack or Flutterwave payment pages) so buyers are not asked to transfer to a personal account they cannot check.
Reply fast. A quick reply message with prices and delivery days often lifts first orders more than a new advert.

blocks.text: Lever 2: respect data costs

Heavy pages and long videos cost your customer money before they have bought anything. Keep landing pages light, compress images, offer a WhatsApp catalogue, and use short voice notes for explanations where customers prefer them. Every step you remove from the path to the first order is a possible activation experiment.
Lever 3: referral loops

A referral loop turns customers into acquisition. You measure it with the **viral coefficient (K)**: the average number of invitations each customer sends multiplied by the share of invitations that become customers. If K is 0.3, every 100 customers bring 30 more, who bring 9 more, and so on. When K is below 1 the loop amplifies your other channels rather than growing on its own, and the total from 100 starting customers is roughly 100 ÷ (1 − K).

blocks.title: Worked example: is the tutoring referral worth it?
blocks.context: For example, Funmi runs paid WAEC and JAMB revision classes for secondary school pupils, sold to parents through WhatsApp in Abuja. She plans to give each referring parent ₦2,000 off next term (illustrative), and only when the friend has paid.
steps: She pilots with 100 parents. On average each shares the invite with 2 other parents.
15% of invited parents enrol. K = 2 × 0.15 = 0.3.
Extra customers from the loop: 100 ÷ (1 − 0.3) = about 143 in total, so about 43 extra parents over several cycles.
Cost: 43 discounts × ₦2,000 = ₦86,000, or ₦2,000 per extra customer.
Her paid-ad CAC is about ₦4,500 (from her own records), so referral customers cost less than half as much.
blocks.result: The referral programme is worth running. Funmi tracks K every term and tests whether a two-sided reward (both parents get ₦1,000 off) raises the share of invites that convert.

blocks.title: Protect customers and your budget
blocks.text: Pay referral rewards only after the new customer's payment clears, and cap rewards per person to stop people inventing fake accounts or referring themselves with a second number. Never ask customers for OTPs, PINs or card details on WhatsApp, and tell them publicly that you never will, because scammers copy popular referral offers.
Other levers worth testing

items: **Community:** a moderated WhatsApp group or Telegram channel for customers can lift retention when it shares useful content, not only adverts.
**Agents and ambassadors:** many fintech and FMCG brands grow through local agents paid per active customer; the same idea works for small brands with campus or market ambassadors.
**Timing:** test sending offers when your customers usually have money, for example soon after month-end salaries, and compare with mid-month.

blocks.text: Growth skills travel well. The same funnel and experiment methods apply whether you work for a Lagos fintech, a Nairobi e-commerce start-up, or remotely for a foreign company. What employers value is proof that you can find a leak, design a fair test and report the result honestly, which the rest of this course builds.
Measuring offline and word-of-mouth growth

Much referral in Nigeria happens offline: in markets, churches and mosques, office groups and family WhatsApp chats. You can still measure it. Give each customer a short personal referral code (for example AMAKA10) to share, ask every new customer "How did you hear about us?" with fixed options, and label the answer in WhatsApp Business. For ambassadors, give each a unique code or link so you can pay only for real paying customers.

Where many customers use basic phones or have little data, consider channels that work without the internet, such as SMS reminders sent with consent, phone calls for high-value orders, or partnering with a business that already offers USSD payments. Each of these is a test: measure the activation or repeat rate for customers reached this way against your usual channel before you invest more.

blocks.name: referral
blocks.alt: People passing an invitation from one phone to another
blocks.caption: A referral loop turns each happy customer into a small acquisition channel.

takeaways: Same funnel, different levers: trust, data cost and payment habits shape the route.
Fewer steps and visible proof usually lift activation.
Viral coefficient K = invites per customer × invite conversion rate.
Below 1, total customers ≈ starting customers ÷ (1 − K); reward only after payment clears.

activity.title: Design a local referral loop
steps: Choose a business and write its current path from first contact to first payment; count the steps.
Remove at least one step and rewrite the path.
Draft a referral offer with a reward paid only after the friend pays, and a cap per person.
Estimate invites per customer and invite conversion, then calculate K and the extra customers from 100 starters.
Write two anti-fraud rules and one customer safety message.
activity.evidence: A short written plan with the old and new activation paths, the referral offer, the K calculation and the safety rules.

quiz.q: A shop had 2,000 website visits, 200 add-to-carts and 50 purchases last month. What is the cart-to-purchase step conversion rate?
quiz.explain: Step rate = this stage ÷ previous stage = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. The 2.5% figure is purchases ÷ visits, the overall rate.

quiz.q: Halima's sales rise only in months when she increases ad spend, and few customers buy twice. What should she investigate first?
options: Retention: why first-time buyers do not return
quiz.explain: Sales that track ad spend, with little repeat buying, signal a retention leak. Scaling acquisition into a leaking funnel wastes money.

quiz.q: A channel cost ₦200,000 and brought 40 new customers. Gross profit per order is ₦2,500 and customers order 4 times a year. What is the LTV to CAC ratio?
Which is the best North Star metric for an online tutoring business?
quiz.explain: Lessons completed reflects value students actually receive and leads to renewals. The others can rise without anyone learning.

quiz.q: Each customer sends 4 invites on average and 10% of invites become customers. Starting from 200 customers, roughly how many customers does the loop produce in total?
Why should a referral reward be paid only after the new customer's payment clears?
options: It is required for business name registration
It reduces fake or self-referrals and protects the budget
It increases data costs for customers
quiz.explain: Paying on cleared payment, with a cap per person, removes the incentive to create fake accounts or refer yourself.

modules.title: The Growth Workflow: Tracking, Experiments and Honest Results
modules.overview: This module gives you the working machinery of growth: a measurement stack you can run from a phone and a laptop, a repeatable experiment loop with ICE and RICE prioritisation and sample-size checks, and the statistical habits that stop you from declaring false wins.

lessons.title: Your growth stack: event tracking, cohort tables and an experiment log
objectives: List the minimum tools needed to measure every AARRR stage
Define the key events a business should track in Google Analytics 4
Build a monthly cohort retention table and read it correctly
Set up an experiment log that records every test, including failures

blocks.text: You cannot improve what you cannot see. A growth stack is the set of tools that records what customers do at each stage, joins it to sales, and stores what you tested. Expensive software is optional. A small business can run a solid stack with free tools and one disciplined spreadsheet.

head: Need
Free or low-cost option
What it gives you
rows: Sessions by source, events such as add_to_cart and purchase, funnel reports
Meta Business Suite and Ads Manager, Instagram Insights
Reach, clicks, cost per result, audience data
Counts of new chats, pending payments, paid orders, repeat buyers
Paystack, Flutterwave, Opay or Moniepoint exports
Real paid orders by date and customer
Google Sheets, optionally Looker Studio for dashboards
Funnel, cohort table, CAC, experiment log in one place

blocks.text: Define events before you need them

In GA4 every action is an **event**. Some are collected automatically (page views, scrolls); others you must set up, such as sign_up, add_to_cart, begin_checkout and purchase. GA4 lets you mark the events that matter most as **key events** (earlier called conversions). Decide your key events from your AARRR map, not from whatever the tool shows by default. For WhatsApp-first sellers, the same idea applies with labels: "New chat", "Price sent", "Paid", "Repeat buyer".

blocks.title: Tracking ready before testing
items: Key events defined per stage
UTM tags on every shared link
Payments matched to customers
Cohort table updated monthly
Experiment log in place
blocks.caption: If any box is unticked, fix tracking first, or your experiment results cannot be trusted.

blocks.text: Cohort tables: the honest view of retention

A **cohort** is a group of customers who started in the same period, for example everyone whose first order was in January. A cohort table shows what share of each group is still buying in later months. It is more honest than total monthly sales, which can rise simply because you bought more ads while old customers quietly disappeared.

blocks.title: Worked example: did the loyalty change work?
blocks.context: For example, Ada (meal prep, Lagos) exports three months of paid orders from Paystack into Google Sheets. She adds a column for each customer's first order month. In February she introduced a free dessert on every fourth order.
steps: January cohort: 80 first-time buyers. In February, 32 of them ordered again: 32 ÷ 80 = 40%. In March, 24 did: 24 ÷ 80 = 30%.
February cohort: 100 first-time buyers. In March, 45 ordered again: 45 ÷ 100 = 45%.
She compares like with like: month-1 retention was 40% for January and 45% for February.
She checks for other causes: no price change, no new ad channel, and February is not a holiday month for her customers.
She records it in her experiment log as "promising, not proven" because it compares only two cohorts and was not a controlled test.
blocks.result: Month-1 retention rose from 40% to 45% after the loyalty change. The cohort view shows the signal clearly; a controlled test (next lesson) is needed to be confident.

blocks.text: The experiment log

Every growth team keeps a log of tests: what was tried, why, and what happened. Without it, teams repeat failed ideas and forget why winning changes were made. Keep one row per experiment with these columns.

items: ID and date started, date ended
Funnel stage and metric targeted
Hypothesis (one sentence)
Priority score (ICE or RICE)
Audience and sample size per group
Result with numbers, decision (scale, iterate, stop), and what you learned

blocks.title: Data privacy
blocks.text: Customer phone numbers and payment exports are personal data under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. Keep sheets private, share view-only links with named people, remove columns you do not need for analysis, and never post screenshots that show customer numbers.
Name your links the same way every time

UTM tags only help if everyone uses the same spelling. Agree a short naming rule and keep it in the first tab of your sheet: lower-case only, utm_source for the platform (instagram, whatsapp, facebook), utm_medium for the type (paid, status, broadcast, bio), and utm_campaign for the offer and month (for example dessert_loyalty_feb). "Instagram", "instagram" and "IG" would otherwise appear in GA4 as three different sources, splitting your numbers.
A weekly measurement routine

items: Monday: export last week's paid orders and update the funnel and cohort tabs (about 20 minutes).
Check that every running experiment is collecting data in both groups.
Note anything unusual: a public holiday, a stock-out, a price change, a delivery problem.
Record the week's numbers in the experiment log so no result depends on memory.

blocks.text: A routine matters more than a fancy dashboard. Ten minutes of honest weekly updating beats a beautiful report that is three months out of date.

blocks.name: mobile-analytics
blocks.alt: A person checking analytics charts on a mobile phone
blocks.caption: Most of a small business's growth stack can be checked from a phone each morning.

takeaways: A free stack (GA4, Meta tools, WhatsApp labels, payment exports, Google Sheets) covers every AARRR stage.
Choose key events from your funnel map before you test anything.
Cohort tables compare like with like and expose retention problems that totals hide.
Log every experiment, including failures, and protect customer data.

activity.title: Build your stack in one sheet
steps: List the key event or label you will use for each AARRR stage.
Export at least two months of paid orders with customer identifiers (remove names you do not need).
Add a first-order-month column and build a cohort table with month-1 and month-2 retention.
Create an experiment log tab with the six column groups from this lesson.
Write one sentence on what your cohort table tells you.
activity.evidence: A Google Sheet with a cohort table tab and an empty experiment log tab, plus your one-sentence reading.

lessons.title: The experiment loop: hypotheses, ICE and RICE scoring, and sample size
objectives: Write a testable hypothesis with a metric, size of change and time frame
Score and rank ideas using ICE and RICE
Estimate the sample size a test needs before launching it
Choose between an A/B test and a before-and-after test

blocks.text: Growth work runs in a loop: analyse, generate ideas, prioritise, test, learn, repeat. The loop matters more than any one idea, because most ideas fail. What separates a professional from someone "trying things" is that every test is chosen deliberately, designed to give a clear answer, and recorded.

blocks.title: The growth experiment loop
items: Analyse the funnel
Generate ideas
Prioritise with ICE or RICE
Design and run the test
Learn and log
blocks.caption: Each lap of the loop starts from what the last test taught you.

blocks.text: Write a hypothesis that can fail

Use this template: **Because we saw [evidence], we believe that [change] for [audience] will increase [metric] from [baseline] to [target] within [time].** A hypothesis that cannot be proven wrong ("better branding will help") is not a hypothesis. For example: "Because 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery days, we believe a quick reply with menu, prices and delivery days for new WhatsApp chats will raise chat-to-order from 30% to 36% within four weeks."
Prioritise: ICE and RICE

**ICE**, popularised by growth marketer Sean Ellis, scores each idea from 1 to 10 on Impact, Confidence and Ease, then averages the three. It is fast and good for small teams. **RICE**, published by the software company Intercom, is more careful: Reach (people affected per period) × Impact (3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal) × Confidence (as a percentage) ÷ Effort (person-weeks).

blocks.title: Worked example: ranking four ideas
blocks.context: For example, Ada has four ideas for her meal-prep business and one free afternoon a week to work on growth.
steps: Quick reply with menu and delivery days: Impact 6, Confidence 8, Ease 10. ICE = (6 + 8 + 10) ÷ 3 = 8.0.
Free dessert on every fourth order: 7, 6, 6. ICE = 19 ÷ 3 = 6.3.
New Instagram ad creative: 5, 5, 7. ICE = 17 ÷ 3 = 5.7.
Build her own mobile app: 8, 3, 2. ICE = 13 ÷ 3 = 4.3.
RICE check on the top two. Quick reply reaches about 900 chats a quarter: 900 × 1 × 0.8 ÷ 0.25 week = 2,880.
Loyalty dessert reaches about 270 repeat-eligible customers a quarter: 270 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 1 week = 270.
blocks.result: Both methods put the quick reply first. The app scores last because effort is high and evidence is thin, even though its imagined impact is large.

blocks.text: How big must the test be?

Small samples produce random swings that look like results. Before launching, estimate the sample you need. A widely used rule of thumb (Lehr's rule) for about 80% power at a 5% significance level is: **people per group ≈ 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d²**, where p is your baseline conversion rate and d is the smallest absolute change you care about. Online calculators such as Evan Miller's sample-size calculator give more exact figures.

blocks.title: Worked example: is this test even possible?
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs an online fabric store in Kano with about 1,800 product-page visitors a month and a 10% add-to-cart rate. She wants to test a new product-photo layout.
steps: To detect a 2-point change (10% to 12%): 16 × 0.10 × 0.90 ÷ 0.02² = 1.44 ÷ 0.0004 = 3,600 visitors per group, 7,200 in total.
At 1,800 visitors a month, that would take 4 months, far too long.
To detect a 4-point change (10% to 14%): 1.44 ÷ 0.0016 = 900 per group, 1,800 in total, about one month.
She decides to test a bold change likely to move the rate a lot, not a small tweak.
blocks.result: Low-traffic businesses should test big, meaningful changes. Tiny button-colour tests need traffic most small businesses do not have.

blocks.text: A/B test or before-and-after?

items: **A/B test:** randomly split people into control (A) and variant (B) at the same time. Best evidence, because both groups face the same week, prices and news. Tools: Meta Ads A/B test feature, email platforms such as Brevo or Mailchimp, or alternating quick replies by chat order.

**Before-and-after:** change everything and compare with a previous period. Easier, but holidays, salary dates and competitor moves can fool you. Compare equal-length periods and note anything unusual.
Run one test per audience at a time, or you will not know which change caused the result.

blocks.title: Decide the rules before you start
blocks.text: Write the metric, the sample size and the end date in your experiment log before launching. Deciding these afterwards invites you to stop the test the day it looks good.

Finally, keep a backlog. Ideas that lose the ranking today are not thrown away: they stay in the log with their scores, and you re-score them after each test, because what you learn changes your confidence. A backlog of twenty scored ideas means you never start a week wondering what to test next.

blocks.name: creative-experiment
blocks.alt: A person mixing ideas in a laboratory flask
blocks.caption: Each growth idea is an experiment: designed in advance, measured fairly, and recorded.

takeaways: Hypothesis: evidence, change, audience, metric, baseline to target, time.
ICE averages Impact, Confidence, Ease; RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort.
Per-group sample ≈ 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d²; low traffic means test big changes.
A/B tests beat before-and-after comparisons; fix the rules before launch.

activity.title: Plan your first proper test
steps: Brainstorm six ideas for the leaking stage you found in Module 1.
Score all six with ICE, then score the top two with RICE.
Write a full hypothesis for the winner using the template.
Calculate the sample size per group and how many weeks your traffic needs.
Choose A/B or before-and-after and record the plan in your experiment log.
activity.evidence: Your experiment log row with hypothesis, scores, sample size, end date and test type filled in before launch.

lessons.title: Reading results honestly: significance, guardrails and ethical growth
objectives: Check whether an A/B result is likely real using a two-proportion z-test
Avoid peeking, novelty effects and seasonal traps
Set guardrail metrics that protect customers and long-term revenue
Run growth experiments that respect consent and data protection law

blocks.text: The most expensive mistake in growth is a false win: you believe a change worked, roll it out, and build on it, when the difference was luck. Honest reading of results is what makes your experiment log trustworthy to an employer or client.
Is the difference real? A simple significance check

For conversion rates, a **two-proportion z-test** compares two groups. Compute each conversion rate, the pooled rate p (all conversions ÷ all people), the standard error SE = √(p × (1 − p) × (1/n₁ + 1/n₂)), and z = difference ÷ SE. If z is above about 1.96 (or below −1.96), the difference is statistically significant at the 5% level. Free online A/B significance calculators do this for you; knowing the steps helps you spot a wrong claim.

blocks.title: Worked example: checkout page test
blocks.context: For example, Amaka tests a shorter checkout page for her Abuja kitchenware store. She randomly splits visitors for 14 days (two full weeks) and agreed the sample size in advance.
steps: Control (A): 2,000 visitors, 100 purchases. Rate = 100 ÷ 2,000 = 5.0%.
Variant (B): 2,000 visitors, 130 purchases. Rate = 130 ÷ 2,000 = 6.5%.
She checks her guardrail: refund requests were 3 in each group, so no harm appeared.
blocks.result: The shorter checkout is a significant win at the 5% level, though only just. Amaka rolls it out and keeps watching purchase rate for the next month to confirm the lift holds.

blocks.text: Traps that create false wins

items: **Peeking:** checking daily and stopping the moment B looks ahead greatly raises the chance of a false win. Stop at the sample size and date you set.
**Too short:** run at least one full week, ideally two, so weekdays and weekends are both included.
**Seasonality:** Ramadan, Easter, December festivities, school resumption and salary dates change buying. Compare groups in the same period, not this month against last.
**Novelty effect:** returning customers may click a new design just because it is new. Check whether the lift lasts after two to four weeks.
**Many metrics:** if you check 20 metrics, about one will look significant by chance at 5%. Name one primary metric in advance.

blocks.title: Real win or false win?
items: Trustworthy result
Warning signs
left: Metric and sample fixed in advance
blocks.caption: Use this check before you report any experiment as a success.

blocks.text: Guardrail metrics

A **guardrail** is a metric that must not get worse while you chase the main one. Aggressive discounts can lift orders but cut gross profit; daily broadcast messages can lift clicks but increase blocks and opt-outs. Typical guardrails: gross margin, refund or complaint rate, unsubscribes or WhatsApp blocks, and delivery time.

blocks.title: Consent and the law
blocks.text: The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent, for processing personal data, and gives people rights over their data. For growth experiments that means: message only people who opted in, make opting out easy, never buy or scrape contact lists, and tell customers how you use their data. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees compliance.

blocks.title: Avoid dark patterns
blocks.text: Fake countdown timers, hidden fees added at checkout, pre-ticked consent boxes and fake "only 2 left" messages can lift short-term numbers while destroying trust. They also expose clients to consumer-protection complaints. Report them as unacceptable, not as clever growth hacks.
What to do with an inconclusive result

Many tests end with no clear winner. That is still useful information: it tells you the change does not have a large effect, so you can stop spending energy on it. Your options are to adopt the cheaper or simpler version if there was no harm, to run the test longer only if you planned that in advance, or to try a bolder variation of the idea. Do not keep extending a test until it happens to cross 1.96.
Writing the result in your log

items: One line on what you tested and for whom.
The numbers for each group, the z value (or calculator output) and the dates.
Guardrail results, including any customer complaints.
Your decision and the reason, in plain words a business owner can follow.
The next question this result raises, which becomes a new idea in the backlog.

blocks.text: When you present to a client, show the raw numbers next to any chart, start the chart axis at zero for rates, and compare the same time period for both groups. These habits make your reports trustworthy, and trust is what keeps a client paying for growth work month after month.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking data entries against a list
blocks.caption: Verifying results before celebrating protects your credibility and your client's money.

takeaways: Use a two-proportion z-test; |z| above about 1.96 means significant at 5%.
Fix sample and end date in advance, run full weeks, and do not peek.
Guardrail metrics protect margin, trust and customer experience.
Consent, easy opt-out and no dark patterns are part of professional growth work.

activity.title: Audit an experiment result
steps: Take a real test you ran, or use the numbers A: 1,500 visitors, 60 sales; B: 1,500 visitors, 75 sales.
Calculate both rates, pooled p, SE and z, showing your working.
Go through the false-win warning signs and note any that apply.
Name two guardrail metrics and record what happened to them (or what you would check).
Write a two-sentence verdict in your experiment log: scale, iterate or stop.
activity.evidence: A worked calculation and a completed experiment log row with verdict and guardrail notes.

quiz.q: Total monthly sales are rising, but the cohort table shows month-1 retention falling from 45% to 30% over three cohorts. What is the best interpretation?
options: The business is healthy because sales are rising
New spending is hiding a retention problem
quiz.explain: Totals can rise because more new customers are bought while existing ones leave. Falling cohort retention is an early warning.

quiz.q: Using ICE, an idea scores Impact 4, Confidence 7, Ease 10. What is its ICE score?
Baseline conversion is 20% and you want to detect a 5-point change. Using Lehr's rule, about how many people do you need per group?
Bisi checks her A/B test every morning and stops on day 3 when B is ahead. What is the main problem?
options: Peeking and stopping early raises the chance of a false win
A/B tests should always run for one day
quiz.explain: Stopping as soon as results look good exploits random swings. Fix the sample size and end date beforehand and run full weeks.

quiz.q: A daily WhatsApp broadcast raised clicks by 20% but blocks doubled. Which concept does this illustrate?
quiz.explain: Blocks are a guardrail. A win on the main metric that damages a guardrail is not a real win.

quiz.q: Which practice is required to run email or WhatsApp experiments in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023?
options: Buy a large contact list to test faster
Message only people with a lawful basis such as consent, and offer easy opt-out
quiz.explain: The Act requires a lawful basis such as consent and respects data subjects' rights; easy opt-out supports that. Bought lists and pre-ticked boxes do not.

modules.title: Growth Consulting: Audits, Proposals and Your Case-Study Portfolio
modules.overview: Now you turn the method into paid work. You will run a discovery session and a growth audit, price and scope an engagement so it stays profitable, and package your own experiments into case studies and a 90-day roadmap that win clients or a growth role.

lessons.title: Discovery and the growth audit: questions, data access and a baseline
objectives: Run a structured discovery call that covers goals, funnel, data and constraints
Request data access safely without taking anyone's passwords
Build a baseline funnel and identify tracking gaps during an audit
Summarise audit findings as a short, prioritised opportunity list

blocks.text: Clients rarely say "please fix my activation rate". They say "sales are slow" or "our ads stopped working". Your first job is diagnosis. A **growth audit** is a short, fixed-scope project: you collect the numbers for each funnel stage, find where tracking is missing, and recommend the first three experiments. It is also the easiest engagement to sell, because it has a clear end and a clear deliverable.

blocks.title: From first call to audit report
items: Discovery call
Data access request
Baseline funnel
Gap and leak analysis
Prioritised recommendations
blocks.caption: Each step produces something the client can see, which builds trust before any experiment runs.

blocks.text: Discovery questions that matter

head: Area
Questions to ask
Why
rows: What would make the next 90 days a success? Which number matters most to you?
Finds the North Star candidate and the real priority
Who buys most often? Why do they choose you? Why do people leave?
Where do customers first hear of you? What happens between first contact and payment?
Maps the actual journey, often different from the website
What do you track today? Who can export payments, ads and analytics data?
Reveals tracking gaps before you promise results
Monthly budget for tests? Who can make changes to the site, catalogue or messages, and how fast?
What have you tried? What happened?
Avoids repeating failures and shows how they make decisions

blocks.title: Listen more than you pitch
blocks.text: Aim to talk for less than a third of the call. Summarise back what you heard at the end: "So your main goal is more repeat orders, and you are not sure where first-time buyers drop off. Is that right?" Clients buy from people who clearly understand their problem.
Getting data access safely

items: Ask to be added as a user with the lowest role that works: for example Viewer or Analyst in Google Analytics, an analyst-level role in Meta Business Suite, and a CSV export of payments rather than a dashboard login.
Never accept a client's personal passwords or OTPs. If they offer, explain that role-based access protects both of you.
Agree in writing (email is fine) what data you will see, how you will store it, and that you will delete or return it when the project ends.
Remove access you no longer need at the end of the engagement and confirm it in your final email.

blocks.title: Protect client and customer data
blocks.text: Payment exports contain names, phone numbers and amounts, which are personal data under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. Store them only in a password-protected account with two-step verification, never on a shared or public computer, and anonymise customer columns before putting any figure in a portfolio.

blocks.title: Worked example: audit of a fashion brand
blocks.context: For example, Zainab owns a ready-to-wear brand in Abuja selling through Instagram, a website and WhatsApp. She says, "Our ads stopped working." You run a 45-minute discovery call and request view-only access.
steps: Ads Manager: ₦300,000 spent last month (illustrative), 6,000 link clicks.
GA4: only 2,100 sessions from Instagram, so about two-thirds of clicks never load the site. Testing on a mid-range phone shows the home page takes a long time to load on mobile data.
Website: 60 orders. WhatsApp labels: 45 more orders from people who chatted instead of checking out, but these were never counted as ad results.
Payments: 105 orders in total, so true CAC from ads is about ₦300,000 ÷ 105 ≈ ₦2,860, not the ₦5,000 the client calculated from website orders alone.
Repeat orders within 60 days: 8%, down from her own earlier months, so retention also needs attention.
blocks.result: The ads were working better than Zainab thought; the problems were a slow landing page, missing WhatsApp attribution and weak retention. Your report recommends three experiments: a lighter landing page, a tracked WhatsApp link with UTM tags, and a post-purchase message series.

blocks.text: Writing the audit summary

Keep the report short: one page of findings, one page of the baseline funnel with numbers and step rates, and one page of three prioritised experiments with ICE scores and expected metric changes. List tracking gaps separately, because fixing measurement is often the first paid task. Clients act on short reports and ignore long ones.
Red flags during discovery

items: The owner cannot say what a customer is worth or how many buy twice: plan tracking work first.
Nobody can approve changes within a week: experiments will stall, so price and schedule for slower cycles.
The client wants guaranteed numbers by a fixed date: explain the process honestly, or decline the work.
Stock or delivery problems are the real cause of lost sales: say so, because marketing cannot fix them.

blocks.name: customer-survey
blocks.alt: A person going through a customer survey form
blocks.caption: Discovery questions and real data together reveal where a client's growth is really stuck.

takeaways: A growth audit is a fixed-scope diagnosis: baseline funnel, tracking gaps, three experiments.
Discovery covers goal, customers, funnel, data, resources and past tests.
Ask for role-based, lowest-level access; never take passwords or OTPs.
Count every channel (including WhatsApp orders) before judging CAC.

activity.title: Run a practice discovery and audit
steps: Find a small business owner willing to be interviewed (a friend's shop is fine).
Run a 30 to 45 minute discovery call using the six areas in the table.
Ask for one month of data in a safe format (CSV exports or view-only access).
Build the baseline funnel with step rates and note every tracking gap.
Write a one-page summary with three prioritised experiments.
activity.evidence: Your call notes (with the owner's permission) and a one-page audit summary.

lessons.title: Pricing, proposals and scope control for growth work
objectives: Compare audit, retainer and embedded engagement models
Calculate a project price from your own hours, rate and costs
Write a proposal with deliverables, timeline, reporting and exclusions
Handle scope changes and payment risks professionally

blocks.text: Growth work is easy to underprice because the visible output, a few changed messages or a landing page, looks small. What the client really buys is diagnosis, prioritisation and honest measurement that stop them wasting money. Price for that value, but build it on a clear calculation so you never work at a loss.

blocks.title: Audit package vs monthly retainer
items: Growth audit
Growth retainer
blocks.caption: Many consultants sell an audit first, then offer a retainer to run the recommended experiments.

blocks.text: Price from your own numbers

Rates vary widely by city, experience and client size, so this course does not give market rates. Instead, set your own day or hourly rate from what you need to earn, the hours you can bill, and your costs (data, software, transport). Then price each project from realistic hours plus a buffer.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing an audit
blocks.context: For example, Kemi, a growth marketer in Port Harcourt, has set her rate at ₦15,000 per hour (her own illustrative figure). A client wants an audit like the one in the last lesson.
steps: Discovery call and notes: 2 hours.
Data access, exports and cleaning: 5 hours.
Baseline funnel, cohort table and CAC by channel: 6 hours.
Report writing and three experiment designs: 5 hours. Presentation call: 2 hours.
Total: 20 hours × ₦15,000 = ₦300,000. Add 15% buffer for revisions and delays: ₦300,000 × 1.15 = ₦345,000.
Payment terms: 50% (₦172,500) before work starts, 50% on delivery of the report.
blocks.result: Kemi quotes ₦345,000 for a three-week audit with a fixed list of deliverables. If the client later wants a retainer, she prices it from the hours per month the experiments will need.

blocks.title: Be careful with pure performance fees
blocks.text: Clients sometimes offer "pay only if sales grow". Growth depends on things you do not control: stock, delivery, prices and the owner's speed. If you agree to any performance element, keep a fixed base fee, define the metric and baseline in writing, and agree how results will be measured before you start.
What a growth proposal includes

items: Your understanding of the problem in the client's own words, from discovery.
Objectives: the metric you will work on and what success looks like, with no guaranteed outcome.
Deliverables: an exact list (for example audit report, cohort table, three experiment designs).
Timeline with dates for each deliverable and the review call.
What the client must provide: data access, a decision-maker, turnaround time for approvals.
Exclusions: for example ad spend, paid tools, design of new products, website rebuilds.
Price, payment schedule, bank or invoice details, and how extra work is charged.

blocks.text: Controlling scope

items: When a client asks for something outside the list, reply warmly and in writing: "Happy to help with that. It is outside the current scope, so I will send a short quote."
Keep a change log of every extra request and its price.
Never promise a specific growth percentage; promise a disciplined process, clear reporting and honest results.

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Be wary of new "clients" who overpay and ask you to refund the difference, or who send screenshots of transfers that never arrive. Confirm money has reached your account in your banking app before starting work, and use a business account with your registered business name where possible.
Pricing a retainer

Price a retainer from the work each month really needs. For example, if running two experiments a month takes Kemi about 8 hours of setup and analysis, 2 hours of reporting and a 1-hour review call, that is 11 hours. At her own rate of ₦15,000 per hour that is ₦165,000 a month before any buffer. She asks for a three-month minimum, because one experiment cycle rarely shows a clear result in less time, and she invoices at the start of each month.

State clearly that advertising budget, paid software and design or printing costs are paid by the client directly, not from your fee. Mixing them makes your income swing with the client's ad spend and can create disputes about money you never kept.
Reporting that keeps clients

items: A short weekly message: what is running, early numbers, anything blocked.
A monthly report: funnel and North Star trend, experiments finished with results, decisions, and next month's plan.
A quarterly review: what changed in unit economics and whether to continue, change focus or end the engagement.
Always include failures and inconclusive tests, with what was learned.

blocks.text: Regular, honest reporting is the main reason clients renew. It also protects you: if growth is slow because approvals or stock were delayed, your written record shows it.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A person reviewing and signing a contract document
blocks.caption: A clear proposal with deliverables and exclusions protects both you and the client.

takeaways: Sell a fixed audit first; offer a retainer to run the experiments.
Price = realistic hours × your rate + buffer; take a deposit before starting.
Proposals list deliverables, timeline, client inputs, exclusions and payment terms.
Never guarantee growth; quote extra work in writing; confirm payments in your own banking app.

activity.title: Draft your audit proposal
steps: Set your hourly rate from your income needs and costs, and write down how you got it.
Estimate the hours for each audit task and add a 15% buffer.
Write a two-page proposal with all seven sections from this lesson.
List at least four exclusions.
Ask a peer to read it and point out anything vague.
activity.evidence: A two-page proposal and your pricing calculation sheet.

lessons.title: Case-study portfolio and a 90-day growth roadmap
objectives: Write a growth case study with baseline, hypothesis, test design, result and learning
Present a failed experiment as evidence of good judgement
Build a 90-day experiment roadmap with weekly rhythm and checkpoints
Plan concrete outreach to win a first client or growth role

blocks.text: Employers and clients hiring for growth do not want a list of tools you have used. They want proof that you can find a leak, test a fix fairly and tell the truth about the result. Two or three well-written case studies do this better than any certificate.
The case-study structure

items: **Context:** the business, its customers and the goal (anonymise if the owner prefers).
**Baseline:** the funnel numbers and step rates before you started.
**Insight:** the evidence that pointed to the leak (for example 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery).
**Hypothesis and design:** the change, the metric, sample size, test type and dates.
**Result:** the numbers for each group, the significance check and guardrails.
**Decision and learning:** what was scaled or stopped and what you would test next.

blocks.title: Worked example: a one-page case study
blocks.context: For example, Ada's meal-prep business from earlier lessons agreed to be featured. Numbers are from her own records and are illustrative here.
steps: Baseline: 300 WhatsApp chats a month, 90 first orders, chat-to-order rate 30%.
Insight: in 30 lost chats, 18 asked about delivery days and waited hours for a reply.
Test: new chats alternated between the old manual reply (A) and a quick reply with menu, prices and delivery days (B) for four weeks.
Result: A had 150 chats and 45 orders (30%); B had 150 chats and 60 orders (40%).
Decision: the lift is promising but not significant at 5%. Because the change is free and caused no complaints, she adopted it and kept measuring for another month.
blocks.result: This case study is strong precisely because it reports an honest, borderline result and a sensible decision. An employer sees judgement, not just a success story.

blocks.title: Failures belong in your portfolio
blocks.text: Include one experiment that did not work, with what you learned. It shows you can read data honestly, which is the rarest skill in growth work.
Your 90-day growth roadmap

A roadmap turns the audit into a plan. Keep it to one page: the North Star and input metrics, the ranked experiment backlog, and a weekly rhythm. A common rhythm is a short weekly growth meeting: review last week's tests, decide, and launch the next ones.

blocks.title: A 90-day growth roadmap
items: Days 1-14: fix tracking, baseline
Days 15-45: first two experiments
Days 46-60: review, scale winners
Days 61-85: next experiments
Days 86-90: report and new plan
blocks.caption: Measurement comes first; experiments follow in cycles with a review in the middle.

blocks.text: From learning to paid work

items: Choose a target: for example Nigerian fintech or e-commerce start-ups, established small brands, or remote growth roles abroad.
Publish your case studies as a simple portfolio page or a PDF you can share on WhatsApp and LinkedIn.
Offer two or three discounted or free audits to local businesses in exchange for permission to publish anonymised results.
Each week, send personalised messages to five to ten target businesses with one specific observation about their funnel.
Track your own outreach like a funnel: messages sent, replies, calls, proposals, signed clients.

blocks.title: Be truthful about your results
blocks.text: Only claim results you measured and the business agreed you can share. Inflated claims are easy to check and end careers quickly.
Presenting the roadmap to a client

Present the roadmap in a short call, not only by email. Start with the one number that matters (the North Star) and where it stands today, then show the biggest leak, the first two experiments and what each needs from the client. End by agreeing the weekly meeting time and who makes decisions. Send a written summary the same day so everyone has the same plan.
Preparing for growth job interviews

items: Expect a funnel case: "Sign-ups are up but revenue is flat. What would you check?" Talk through AARRR, retention and data quality before suggesting ideas.
Expect simple numbers: CAC, LTV, conversion rates and sample size. Practise doing them aloud.
Bring one case study you can explain in two minutes, including what went wrong.
Ask about their experiment process and tracking; it shows you understand how growth really works.

blocks.text: Whether you choose clients or employment, keep running small experiments on your own outreach and portfolio. Your skill improves fastest when you apply the loop to yourself: measure, test, learn and record.

Keep each case study to one page with the key numbers in a small table, so a busy reader can understand it in two minutes. Add a short note on your role, for example 'designed the test and analysed results; the owner sent the messages', so nobody can say you claimed work that was not yours.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A person arranging projects on a portfolio website
blocks.caption: A small portfolio of honest case studies is your strongest proof of growth skill.

takeaways: Case study: context, baseline, insight, hypothesis and design, result, decision and learning.
Report borderline and failed results honestly; it shows judgement.
90-day roadmap: tracking first, experiments in cycles, mid-point review, final report.
Treat your own outreach as a funnel and measure it.

activity.title: Write your first case study and roadmap
steps: Pick the experiment you planned in Module 2 (or a completed one) and write it up in the six-part structure.
Calculate and include the significance check.
Build a one-page 90-day roadmap for the same business.
List ten target businesses or roles and draft your first outreach message.
Ask the business owner for written permission before publishing anything.
activity.evidence: One case study page, one 90-day roadmap page and a list of ten targets with your outreach draft.

quiz.q: A client offers to send you her Meta account password so you can check her ads. What should you do?
options: Ask her to add you as a user with an analyst-level role instead
Ask for her OTP as well
Refuse to look at ads data
quiz.explain: Role-based access with the lowest level that works protects both of you. Never take personal passwords or OTPs.

quiz.q: Ads Manager shows 4,000 clicks but GA4 shows only 1,300 sessions from that campaign. What is the most likely issue to investigate first?
options: Many visitors leave before the page loads, or tracking is broken
quiz.explain: A large gap between clicks and sessions usually points to slow mobile loading or missing tracking. Test page speed on a mid-range phone and check the tags.

quiz.q: Your audit has 24 estimated hours at ₦12,000 per hour, plus a 15% buffer. What is the price?
Midway through a retainer, the client asks you to also redesign their logo. What is the professional response?
options: Do it free to keep them happy
Note it is outside scope and send a short written quote
quiz.explain: Scope control means acknowledging the request warmly, confirming it is extra, and pricing it in writing.

quiz.q: In a case study, group A converted 45 of 150 and group B 60 of 150, with z ≈ 1.82. How should you report it?
options: As a promising lift that was not significant at the 5% level, with the decision taken
Leave it out of the portfolio
Change the numbers so z is above 1.96
quiz.explain: z is below 1.96, so the result is not significant at 5%. Reporting it honestly with a sensible decision shows good judgement.

quiz.q: Which order best fits a 90-day growth roadmap?
options: Fix tracking and baseline, run experiments in cycles, review mid-way, report
Scale ads first, then fix tracking
Run ten experiments at once in week 1
Write the final report before testing
quiz.explain: Measurement must come first so results can be trusted; experiments then run in cycles with a review point.

finalQuiz.q: Which list gives the five AARRR stages?
finalQuiz.explain: Dave McClure's pirate metrics are Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral and Revenue.

finalQuiz.q: A funnel shows 500 chats, 100 first orders and 20 repeat buyers. What is the first-order-to-repeat step rate?
finalQuiz.explain: Step rate = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%. 4% is repeat buyers ÷ chats.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the strongest North Star metric for a thrift-savings app?
options: Users who made a deposit this month
finalQuiz.explain: Deposits reflect real value delivered and lead revenue; downloads and likes can rise without anyone saving.

finalQuiz.q: Spend ₦240,000 brought 60 customers. Gross profit per order is ₦3,000 and customers order 2 times a year. Which is true?
finalQuiz.explain: CAC = 240,000 ÷ 60 = ₦4,000. LTV = 3,000 × 2 = ₦6,000. Ratio 6,000 ÷ 4,000 = 1.5 to 1, too weak to scale aggressively.

finalQuiz.q: Each customer invites 3 people and 10% join. With 300 starting customers, about how many customers does the loop give in total?
Why is a cohort table better than total monthly sales for judging retention?
options: It compares groups who started at the same time, so new buying cannot hide churn
finalQuiz.explain: Cohorts follow the same customers over time, revealing drop-off that rising totals can hide.

finalQuiz.q: An idea has Reach 1,000 per quarter, Impact 2, Confidence 50% and Effort 2 person-weeks. What is its RICE score?
Baseline conversion is 5% and a business has 600 visitors a month. What is the best testing approach?
options: Test bold changes likely to cause large differences, or use longer periods
finalQuiz.explain: With low traffic, sample-size maths shows only large effects can be detected in reasonable time.

finalQuiz.q: A: 1,000 visitors, 50 sales. B: 1,000 visitors, 70 sales. Pooled p = 0.06 and SE ≈ 0.0106. What is z and the verdict?
finalQuiz.explain: Difference = 0.07 − 0.05 = 0.02. z = 0.02 ÷ 0.0106 ≈ 1.88, below 1.96, so not significant at the 5% level.

finalQuiz.q: Which is a guardrail metric when testing bigger discounts?
finalQuiz.explain: Discounts can lift orders while cutting profit, so gross margin must be watched alongside the main metric.

finalQuiz.q: During an audit, the client's website shows 60 orders but payments show 105, because many buyers paid after chatting on WhatsApp. What should you do?
options: Count all paid orders by source and fix WhatsApp attribution
Tell the client their ads failed
finalQuiz.explain: True CAC uses all orders the ads produced. Missing WhatsApp attribution is a tracking gap to fix first.

finalQuiz.q: What is the strongest portfolio evidence for a growth marketer?
options: A promise to double any client's sales
Case studies with baseline, hypothesis, fair test, honest result and decision

capstone.title: Growth Marketing Experiment Plan
capstone.brief: For a real or practice business (with the owner's permission), produce a funnel analysis that identifies the biggest growth opportunity, one documented experiment with hypothesis, method, success metric and honest result, and a prioritised 90-day experiment roadmap.
steps: Agree access and data handling with the business owner in writing.
Build the AARRR funnel with one month of numbers, step rates, CAC by channel and a cohort table.
Interview the owner and read at least 20 customer conversations from the weakest stage.
Generate at least six experiment ideas and rank them with ICE, then RICE for the top two.
Run one experiment with sample size, metric, guardrails and end date fixed in advance.
Analyse the result with a significance check and write it up as a six-part case study.
Build a one-page 90-day roadmap and present it to the owner.
evidence: Funnel sheet with stage numbers, step rates, CAC per channel and a cohort table
Experiment log row completed before launch and after the result
One-page 90-day roadmap and the owner's written feedback
